introduction.p:
Suppose we have a basis for \real^2 consisting of the vectors
\vvec_1=\twovec11,\hspace{24pt} \vvec_2=\twovec02
as shown in . Notice that this basis is not orthogonal.

image.shortdescription: Two vectors in the two dimensional coordinate plane that are not orthogonal to one another.

description.p: Two vectors \vvec_1=\twovec11 and \vvec_2=\twovec02 against a 1\times1 standard coordinate grid and set of axes.

statement.p: Find the vector \vhat_2 that is the orthogonal projection of \vvec_2 onto the line defined by \vvec_1.

solution.p: The orthogonal projection \vhat_2 is defined so that \vvec_2-\vhat_2 is orthogonal to \vvec_1.

statement.p: Define the new vectors \wvec_1=\vvec_1 and \wvec_2=\vvec_2-\vhat_2 and sketch them in . Explain why \wvec_1 and \wvec_2 define an orthogonal basis for \real^2.
You can upload a scan of your sketch below.

image.shortdescription: A two dimensional coordinate grid and set of axes.

description.p: A 1\times1 coordinate grid and set of axes. The horizontal and vertical ranges run from -3 to 3.

solution.p: \wvec_1 = \twovec11 and \wvec_2=\twovec{-1}1 are othogonal, which can be checked with the dot product.

statement.p: Write the vector \bvec=\twovec8{-10} as a linear combination of \wvec_1 and \wvec_2.
Scale the vectors \wvec_1 and \wvec_2 to produce an orthonormal basis \uvec_1 and \uvec_2 for \real^2.
